# Representation-Enhanced Cascading Multi-Level Interest Learning for Multi-Behavior Recommendation

HU LIU, School of Big Data & Software Engineering, Chongqing University, Chongqing, China XIAO HUANG, College of Computer and Information Science, Southwest University, Chongqing, China WEI ZHOU, School of Big Data & Software Engineering, Chongqing University, Chongqing, China FENGJI LUO, School of Civil Engineering, The University of Sydney, Sydney, Australia JUNHAO WEN and HONGYU ZHANG, School of Big Data & Software Engineering, Chongqing

University, Chongqing, China

Multi-behavior recommendation leverages multiple user-item interaction information to alleviate data sparsity. Although different types of user-item interactions are temporally mutually exclusive, the sequence of behavioral interactions consisting of multi-level positive feedback signals contains rich information. However, most existing studies have unilaterally focused on the positive utility of auxiliary behaviors, ignoring multi-level user preference information. Effectively fusing multi-behavioral data and better modeling behavioral dependencies are urgent problems that need to be addressed for multi-behavior recommendation. We propose the parallel learning of positive and negative interests with an auxiliary-view representation enhancement (PPN-ARE) scheme for multi-level user interest learning based on multi-behavioral interaction sequences. Specifically, multi-level positive and negative feedback view chains are constructed from multi-behavioral sequence data to learn multi-level user interests. User preference evolution is simulated during multi-behavior interactions using residual connections, and the shortcomings of the cascading structure used for higher-order graph learning are analytically highlighted. The influence of low-quality embeddings of auxiliary behaviors is filtered, and the learning of target behaviors is optimized by designing a representation enhancement layer. Finally, the model is optimized using a multi-task training framework. The experimental results indicate that PPN-ARE significantly improved over the state-of-the-art (SOTA). The open source code is available at https://github.com/lhybq/PPN-ARE.

Syst. 44, 2, Article 49 (January 2026), 31 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3786341 ## 1 Introduction Recommender systems filter information by predicting user ratings or preferences toward items \( \left\lbrack {{14},{26},{29}}\right\rbrack \) ,emerging as one of the primary solutions to the problem of information overload. In particular, collaborative filtering epitomizes the rapid evolution of modern recommender systems \( \left\lbrack {{12},{36}}\right\rbrack \) ,plays an increasingly pivotal role in areas such as social news [49] and e-commerce \( \left\lbrack {1,9,{11}}\right\rbrack \) , and has progressively become one of the critical issues in the domain of computer science \( \left\lbrack {{38},{40},{48}}\right\rbrack \) . Previously, recommender systems have been predominantly considered to exhibit a single behavior [12, 36], focusing solely on buying interactions in e-commerce platforms. Later studies recognized that such recommendation models might suffer from data sparsity issues and introduced multi-behavioral data to enrich the data. In addition to the target behavior (e.g., buying), auxiliary actions such as clicking, collecting, and adding to cart are considered. The shared philosophy behind these multi-behavior recommendation methods is that user interactions beyond the mainly targeted behavior may encapsulate valuable information \( \left\lbrack {4,7,{44}}\right\rbrack \) . How to model the relationships among various behaviors and integrate auxiliary behavior information to enhance recommendation performance has always been a crucial challenge in multi-behavior recommendation research. Previous studies on behavioral dependency modeling for graph convolutional network (GCN)-based multi-behavior recommendation can be divided into two categories. One category models multi-behavior interactions as heterogeneous graphs and focuses on message-passing and graph convolution updates on these graphs, as shown in Figure 1(a). The other category focuses on multi-behavior recommendations at the embedding level by learning user and item embeddings from behaviors and then employing different strategies to aggregate the learned embeddings [15, 42, 43], as shown in Figure 1(b). Recent studies [4, 34, 44] proposed the third multi-behavior modeling approach, utilizing cascading GCN for information prediction, as shown in Figure 1(c). The idea of this category is that the sequence of user-item interaction behaviors implies different levels of user preferences for the target item. Unlike NMTR [7], which takes into account the connections between different behaviors, CRGCN [44] employs a cascading residual graph convolution network, allocating a separate convolution block for each type of behavior and learning the features of behavior interaction data based on the residual output of the preceding block. In addition,several studies \( \left\lbrack {4,{22},{45}}\right\rbrack \) have focused on the necessity of information bias correction and preference alignment when making predictions of target behaviors based on preferences learned separately from different behaviors. Motivation. The cascading residual model discards the aggregation strategy from a global perspective \( \left\lbrack {{11},{15},{42},{43}}\right\rbrack \) and avoids complex aggregation design by directly modeling behavioral dependencies based on observing the behavioral interaction order [4, 44]. However, works such as CRGCN [44] face two main issues. First, the modeling of behavioral dependencies is incomplete. Existing works [4, 44] utilized multi-behavior positive feedback to model positive dependencies. Contrarily, multi-behavior interaction sequences contain multiple levels of positive and negative feedback signals, as shown in Figure 2, where behavioral patterns such as clicking-not adding cart-not buying, clicking-adding cart-not buying, which contain negative feedback signals, help model behavioral dependencies and learn user preferences. Second, existing works [4, 44] utilized multi-behavior positive feedback to model positive dependencies [4, 22], and the effect of upstream behaviors greatly affects the learning of preferences on subsequent behaviors. Furthermore, this structure emphasizes linear dependencies between behaviors, and the importance of the target behavior in preference learning is insufficient. In addition, there is a lack of work that addresses the problem by thinking in terms of representational optimization.

For a specific behavior, the user and item dimensions are mapped to the interaction data for that behavior. For specific users and items, interaction data across different behaviors is mapped to the user's behavior pattern. Our Method. To remedy these deficiencies, by modeling more complete behavioral dependencies and optimizing inter-behavioral embedding transfer, we implement an augmented residual cascading graph convolution network for multi-behavior recommendation, which uses a residual design to depict behavioral connections. Specifically, in addition to the existing positive user preference learning, we design negative behavioral view generation strategies and construct cascading view structures to extract multi-level negative feedback signals, which are used to learn users' negative preferences in parallel. Moreover, to alleviate the problem of low-quality representation and enhance the learning effect of the target behavior, we embed a representation optimization layer before the target behavior residual block and devise an optimization objective. The model learns multi-level user interest profiles, using uninterested ratings to filter and enhance final recommendations based on interested ratings, thereby improving recommendation quality. We conducted extensive experimental analysis on real-world datasets. According to several evaluation metrics, our model considerably outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) of multi-behavior recommendation. Comprehensive ablation studies and variant experiments further validate the efficacy of each module in our model.

Contributions. Overall, the primary contributions of our work can be summarized as follows: - Cascading Feature Enhancement: We construct cascading views of positive and negative behaviors and use a residual design to model the hierarchical relationship between behavioral feedback signals to develop a positive and negative interest learning model based on cascading residual networks. - Cascading Representation Optimization: We enhance the learning capability of cascading residual graph convolution networks with an embedded representation optimization layer to address the problem of low-quality representation transfer and propose a new approach to strengthen the focus on target behavior learning. - Experimental Findings: We conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets to validate the effectiveness of the proposed model. We have also made the experimental code and data publicly available to facilitate reproducibility. The remainder of this article is organized as follows: Section 2 describes the motivation for our work in more detail. Sections 3 and 4 provide a detailed description of the parallel learning of positive and negative interests with auxiliary-view representation enhancement (PPN-ARE). Section 5 discusses the experimental setups and analyses. Section 6 reviews relevant research advancements. Section 7 presents the conclusion and prospects. ## 2 Motivation In this section, we first quantify the number of multi-level features of interest under the behavioral cascade structure and then conduct experiments to explore the challenges posed by the multi-level distribution of features in this structure for target-task learning. ### 2.1 Quantification of Feedback Signal Features in the Cascading Behavioral Perspective Most existing multi-behavioral recommendations directly utilize positive feedback information from interaction data, as shown in Figure 1, and various models learn user preferences directly from this positive feedback. However, as shown in Figure 2, multi-behavioral interaction data are highly hierarchical and contain rich feedback information at each level, including both positive and negative feedback. Modeling multi-behavioral interactions between users and items in a cascading structure draws our attention to the importance of behavioral bipolarity. Specifically, in previous single-graph modeling approaches, such as those in Figure 1(a) and (b), positive behavioral feedback is given much higher priority than negative behavioral feedback in the preference learning of individual behavior. However, in the cascading modeling approach of Figure 1(c), the preference learning between behaviors is cascading, and the negative feedback for a behavior is not only a reflection of the preference of the current behavior but, more importantly, a refinement of the preference of the previous behavior. For example,in the behavioral pattern of viewing \( > \) adding to cart \( > \) buying, the user views the item. Still, in the second level of interaction view, the user does not add the item to the cart, so the negative feedback is not only a reflection of the behavioral preference for adding to the cart, but also a refinement of the behavioral pattern preference for viewing behavior.

Fig. 3. Quantifying multi-level feedback features in multi-behavioral interaction data. (a) In multi-behavioral interaction datasets, distinct hierarchical features emerge in the user-item interaction data due to the order in which behaviors are generated, and these features can be categorized into positive and negative feedback. As shown in Figure 3(a), with the cascading structure, there are positive and negative feedback signal features corresponding to each auxiliary behavior in both the Tmall and Beibei datasets. Further, we quantified the feedback signal features at each level. As shown in Figure 3(b) and (c), on average, negative feedback can account for nearly 40% of the total feedback signals at each level, which significantly exceeds the number of target interactions. For example, in the Beibei dataset, the number of negative feedback events generated by viewing but not adding to cart is 1,769,964 which is 5.8 times the number of target behavioral interactions. Similarly, this multiple reaches 6.0 in the Tmall dataset. Therefore, we plan to leverage this feedback to cascade multi-behavioral modeling and improve its recommendation performance. ### 2.2 Investigating the Impact of Low-Quality Features in Cascade View Structure on Recommendation Accuracy In this section, we conduct a preliminary experimental investigation on the recommendation performance of cascading multi-graph models (e.g., CRGCN [44]) on the Beibei and Tmall datasets. We employ a cascade structure to implement the multi-behavior recommendation task, based on the phenomenon and assumption that multiple behavioral interactions may occur between users and items, with various auxiliary behaviors preceding the target behavior in an orderly fashion, as shown in Figure 2(a). This sequential difference in behaviors reflects the differences in user preferences underlying the various behaviors, such as starting to view items, then adding items of interest to the cart and finally buying the most desired items. These three behaviors reflect the user's preference for items from weak to strong and project user preferences through behavioral patterns. Specifically, the cascade structure directly models this behavioral pattern, e.g., on the Beibei dataset, the cascade structure model first learns the user's primary preference on the viewing interaction view, then inputs the learned preference into the add-to-cart interaction view to strengthen the preference, and then finally learns the preference by using the buying view, which is the target behavior. Although the cascade modeling approach achieves SOTA results, it also poses some problems. In the Beibei dataset,user behavioral interactions strictly follow the order of viewing \( > \) adding to cart \( > \) buying. Among the total interaction records,viewing interactions are the first to be generated, accounting for nearly 72% (e.g., Table 2), which significantly determines the overall effectiveness of the recommendation task. Additionally, in the behavioral cascade structure, the learning effect of the target behavior is also limited by the learning of upstream behaviors, such as viewing behavior.

By observing the experimental effects, we find that higher-order preference learning on upstream behavioral views is instead detrimental to the target behavioral recommendation effect. Noting that LightGCN [12] argues that higher-order behavioral learning promotes recommendation effectiveness, the experimental results thus corroborate our argument that the learning effect on upstream behaviors significantly affects the learning effect on downstream target behaviors and ultimately shapes the overall recommendation effect and that the priority and importance of target behaviors are not fully emphasized in the cascade structure. ## 3 Preliminaries ### 3.1 Problem Formulation In practice, multi-behavior recommendation leverages the presence of multiple non-target interactions (e.g., clicking, adding to cart) to help predict target behavior (e.g., buying). Multiple behaviors present a cascading order in the time dimension, reflecting changes in user interest that occur before the target behavioral interaction. The overall recommendation task can be described as follows: Input. Multi-behavior interaction sequence list \( \mathcal{B} \) ,bipartite graph sequence \( \mathcal{G} = \left\lbrack {{\mathcal{G}}_{1},{\mathcal{G}}_{2},\ldots ,{\mathcal{G}}_{K}}\right\rbrack \) , user set \( \mathcal{U} \) ,and item set \( \mathcal{I} \) . Output. Based on user-item embedding similarity, provide a target interaction prediction score for each user-item pair to measure the likelihood of the target behavior (e.g., buying) occurring. Based on the score ordering, generate a top-k composed list of recommended items for each user. ### 3.2 Definition Formulation We briefly explain the definitions of the terms and a table (Table 1) of the symbols involved.

Definition 1 (Multi-Behavior Chain). Considering the sequential order of multiple behavioral interactions,we formally fix this order; that is,an interaction behavior \( {\mathcal{B}}_{i} \) precedes \( {\mathcal{B}}_{j} \) when \( i < j \) . For instance,a clicking event happens before an item is added to favorites. It is described in the list \( \mathcal{B} \) . Definition 2 (Behavior Pattern). There is a chain of behaviors between user \( \left( {u \in \mathcal{U}}\right) \) and item \( \left( {i \in \mathcal{I}}\right) \) ,such as clicking,adding to cart,and buying. The interaction between \( u \) and \( i \) occurs when the user clicks on \( i \) and adds it to the cart,but does not buy it. The behavioral pattern between \( u \) and \( i \) can be described by the sequence 1-1-0,as shown in Figure 2(b). ## 4 Methodology Before users decide on the final targeted action, they have already made choices related to auxiliary behavioral interactions [32]. We use a behavioral view cascading residual structure to capture feedback signals and enhance multi-level feedback features, from which we learn the user's positive and negative interests and obtain enhanced embeddings. As shown in Figure 5, PPN-ARE consists of three main components. Generating positive and negative behavioral view chains (I and II) captures users' affirmative and adverse feedback about items. Parallel cascading residual structures (III) are designed to learn the positive and negative embeddings of users and items from the behavioral view chain. An embedding optimization layer (IV) enhances the representation quality relevant to target behavior learning. In this section, three subsections, including Sections 4.1-4.3, are used to describe each of the three main components of the PPN-ARE, and Section 4.4 is used to detail the training process of PPN-ARE to perform the recommendation task. ### 4.1 Positive and Negative View Chain Initially, we define the multi-behavior chain and subsequently elaborate on its construction based on positive and negative feedback. Considering the sequential order of multiple behavioral interactions, we formally fix this order and define a multi-behavior chain. For a particular behavior \( {\mathcal{B}}_{k} \) ,the collection of all user-item interaction records constitutes the bipartite interaction graph, denoted as \( {\mathcal{G}}_{k} \) ,which corresponds to the 0-1 interaction matrix \( {\mathcal{W}}_{k} \) . Considering \( K \) types of behaviors,we form a sequence of 0-1 interaction matrices of length \( K \) ,represented as \( \mathcal{W} = \left\lbrack {{\mathcal{W}}_{1},{\mathcal{W}}_{2},\ldots ,{\mathcal{W}}_{K}}\right\rbrack \) . 4.1.1 Generation of Positive Interest View. The original user behavior data with positive feedback forms the positive interest view chain, which includes the multi-behavior chain of viewing, adding to cart,and buying. An interaction between a user and an item in behavior \( {\mathcal{B}}_{k} \) is considered to be positive feedback. For the behavior sequence \( \mathcal{B} \) ,each user has a binary interaction sequence for every item. Considering all user-item pairs,as shown in Figure 2(b),there are \( M \times N \) binary interaction sequences, where the third dimension models the interaction process that reflects individual interest tendencies. The first and second dimensions align with interaction behaviors, indicating collaborative information between users. Considering the collaborative relationship in behaviors,for behavior \( {\mathcal{B}}_{k} \) ,all user-item pairs with interactions form the positive feedback view for that behavior,which leads to the creation of the interaction matrix \( {\mathcal{P}}_{k} \) . In essence, \( {\mathcal{W}}_{k} = {\mathcal{P}}_{k} \) . Furthermore,the positive feedback interaction matrices \( {\mathcal{P}}_{k} \) for all behaviors form the positive interest view chain \( \left\lbrack {{\mathcal{P}}_{1},{\mathcal{P}}_{2},\ldots ,{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}\right\rbrack \) ,which is essentially equal to \( \mathcal{W} \) . This is used to sequentially learn about the users' positive interests. 4.1.2 Generation of Negative Interest View. Users' multi-behavior interactions encompass both positive feedback and negative reactions toward items. For instance, consider user interaction data such as viewing-not adding to cart-not buying or viewing-adding to cart-not buying. Based on the behavior chain definition and the inheritable relationship among user behaviors, if a specific user-item interaction has no subsequent interactions in the behavior chain, it is treated as negative feedback, suggesting that the user has a negative interest in that item. Specifically, if there is an interaction between a user and an item in \( {\mathcal{B}}_{k} \) ,but no interactions in \( { \cup }_{i = k + 1}^{K}{\mathcal{B}}_{i} \) ,it is regarded as negative feedback. Considering multi-level feedback from the behavior chain, we construct negative feedback interaction views for \( K - 1 \) behaviors. As a result,a chain of negative interest views is generated to learn the negative interest of the user. The negative feedback interaction matrix \( {\mathcal{B}}_{k} \) over the behavior \( {\mathcal{N}}_{k} \) is defined as follows:

\[{\mathcal{N}}_{k} = \left( {\operatorname{sgn}\left( {-\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = k + 1}}^{K}{\mathcal{W}}_{j}}\right) + 1}\right) \odot {\mathcal{W}}_{k} \tag{2}\] Fig. 5. ### 4.2 Parallel Cascading Residual GCN We separately learn user preferences on the positive and negative interest behavior chains. We learn the collaborative signals within each behavior interaction using the simple single-layer LightGCN [12] model. On the multi-behavior chain, we design residuals to continuously learn and reinforce user preferences [44]. In this work, we employ common initialization methodologies from existing recommendation systems [7, 12, 15]. User and item IDs are utilized to initialize the positive and negative interest embeddings, \( e \) and \( v \) ,which serve as the initial inputs for the residual behavior chain GCN. Specifically, \( {e}_{u}^{0} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d} \) and \( {v}_{u}^{0} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d} \) represent the initial embeddings for user \( u \in \mathcal{U} \) ,whereas \( {e}_{i}^{0} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d} \) and \( {v}_{i}^{0} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d} \) represent the initial embeddings for item \( i \in \mathcal{I} \) ,where \( d \) denotes the embedding dimension. 4.2.1 GCN on Behavior View Chains. GCN has been widely applied in recommendation systems \( \left\lbrack {{12},{20},{36},{46}}\right\rbrack \) . In this work,we employ GCN operations to learn behavioral characteristics from individual interaction data. Specifically, we use the operations of LightGCN [12] to aggregate neighborhood information to learn user preferences for the current behavior \( {\mathcal{B}}_{k} \) . Updating of positive and negative embeddings is described as follows: \[{e}_{u}^{k,l + 1} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i \in {N}_{u}^{p}}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\left| {N}_{u}^{p}\right| }\sqrt{\left| {N}_{i}^{p}\right| }}{e}_{i}^{k,l},\;{e}_{i}^{k,l + 1} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{u \in {N}_{i}^{p}}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\left| {N}_{i}^{p}\right| }\sqrt{\left| {N}_{u}^{p}\right| }}{e}_{u}^{k,l}, \tag{4}\] \[{v}_{u}^{k,l + 1} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i \in {N}_{u}^{n}}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\left| {N}_{u}^{n}\right| }\sqrt{\left| {N}_{i}^{n}\right| }}{v}_{i}^{k,l},\;{v}_{i}^{k,l + 1} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{u \in {N}_{i}^{n}}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\left| {N}_{i}^{n}\right| }\sqrt{\left| {N}_{u}^{n}\right| }}{v}_{u}^{k,l},\] where \( {e}_{u}^{k,l},{e}_{i}^{k,l} \) are the user and item embeddings after the \( l \) th layer neighborhood aggregation on \( {\mathcal{P}}_{k} \) ,respectively,and \( {v}_{u}^{k,l},{v}_{i}^{k,l} \) are the embeddings on \( {\mathcal{N}}_{k} \) ,correspondingly. \( {N}_{u}^{p} \) and \( {N}_{i}^{p} \) denote the set of items interacting with user \( u \) and the set of users interacting with item \( i \) in the behavior \( {\mathcal{B}}_{k} \) , respectively. \( {N}_{u}^{n} \) and \( {N}_{i}^{n} \) denote the set of items associated with user \( u \) and the set of users associated with item \( i \) in the negative interest view \( {\mathcal{N}}_{k} \) ,respectively. Notably,we discard the multi-layer signal linear aggregation in LightGCN [12] to simplify the model and alleviate oversmoothing, while avoiding the discussion of the design of multi-behavior GCN layer number [44]. That means the value of \( l \) in Equation (4) is 0 . Therefore,the positive and negative embedding outputs after the graph convolution operation on a single view block are denoted as follows: (5) \[{e}_{u}^{k} = {\widetilde{e}}_{u}^{k,1} + {e}_{u}^{k,0} = \frac{{e}_{u}^{k,1}}{{\begin{Vmatrix}{e}_{u}^{k,1}\end{Vmatrix}}_{2}} + {e}_{u}^{k,0},\;{e}_{i}^{k} = {\widetilde{e}}_{i}^{k,1} + {e}_{i}^{k,0} = \frac{{e}_{i}^{k,1}}{{\begin{Vmatrix}{e}_{i}^{k,1}\end{Vmatrix}}_{2}} + {e}_{i}^{k,0},\] \[{v}_{u}^{k} = {\widetilde{v}}_{u}^{k,1} + {v}_{u}^{k,0} = \frac{{v}_{u}^{k,1}}{{\begin{Vmatrix}{v}_{u}^{k,1}\end{Vmatrix}}_{2}} + {v}_{u}^{k,0},\;{v}_{i}^{k} = {\widetilde{v}}_{i}^{k,1} + {v}_{i}^{k,0} = \frac{{v}_{i}^{k,1}}{{\begin{Vmatrix}{v}_{i}^{k,1}\end{Vmatrix}}_{2}} + {v}_{i}^{k,0},\] where \( {e}_{u}^{k},{e}_{i}^{k} \) and \( {v}_{u}^{k},{v}_{i}^{k} \) are the final embeddings outputted by the residual block of positive and negative view chain for the behavior \( {\mathcal{B}}_{k} \) ,which include the initial user and item input embeddings \( {e}_{u}^{k,0},{e}_{i}^{k,0},{v}_{u}^{k,0},{v}_{i}^{k,0} \) and the \( {L}_{2} \) normalized user and item embeddings \( {\widetilde{e}}_{u}^{k,1},{\widetilde{e}}_{i}^{k,1},{\widetilde{v}}_{u}^{k,1},{\widetilde{v}}_{i}^{k,1} \) acquired through a single layer of GCN. Normalization is implemented to prevent disparities in embedding magnitudes caused by differences in data across varying behavior views. 4.2.2 Residual Cascading Transmission Between Interest Views. Using the residuals, the learning of the GCN on the behavior view chain is cascaded, and the output of the previous behavior's GCN block is used as the input for the next behavior's GCN learning [44]. Thus, in Equation (5), \( {e}_{u}^{k,0},{e}_{i}^{k,0} \) are replaced by \( {e}_{u}^{k - 1} \) and \( {e}_{i}^{k - 1} \) . On the positive behavior view chain,the embedding update equations for each view are described as follows:

\[{e}_{u}^{k} = {\widetilde{e}}_{u}^{k,1} + {e}_{u}^{k - 1},\;{e}_{i}^{k} = {\widetilde{e}}_{i}^{k,1} + {e}_{i}^{k - 1}, \tag{6}\] where \( {e}_{u}^{k} \) and \( {e}_{i}^{k} \) denote the embeddings of users and items after domain aggregation in the positive view \( {\mathcal{P}}_{k} \) . Likewise,on the negative behavior view chain,the embedding update equations for each view are described as follows: \[{v}_{u}^{k} = {\widetilde{v}}_{u}^{k,1} + {v}_{u}^{k - 1},\;{v}_{i}^{k} = {\widetilde{v}}_{i}^{k,1} + {v}_{i}^{k - 1}, \tag{7}\] where \( {v}_{u}^{k} \) and \( {v}_{i}^{k} \) denote the embeddings of users and items after learning in the negative view \( {\mathcal{N}}_{k} \) . ### 4.3 Optimization of Auxiliary Behavior Representations By cascading user-item embeddings through residual learning, we continually learn and reinforce user preferences while also propagating data bias issues [4]. Furthermore, directly embedding the learning of auxiliary behaviors into the target behavior does not fully capture the target behavior's priority. We introduce CL between cascaded multi-behavior views, design a representation optimization layer before the target behavior residual block to optimize low-quality representations, and enhance target learning effects. CL is effective in mitigating data issues [19, 23, 39] and enhancing the quality of representation embeddings [33, 47, 49]. It has been widely applied in collaborative filtering-based recommendation systems and has been gradually introduced into multi-behavior recommendation methods such as S-MBRec [8] and IICL [18]. CL employs the infoNCE loss as the learning objective. \[{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{ infoNCE }} = {\mathbb{E}}_{\left( {x,y}\right) \sim {\mathrm{p}}_{\text{ pos }}}\left\lbrack {-\log \frac{{e}^{f{\left( x\right) }^{T}f\left( y\right) /\tau }}{{e}^{f{\left( x\right) }^{T}f\left( y\right) /\tau } + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{e}^{f{\left( {x}_{i}^{ - }\right) }^{T}f\left( x\right) /\tau }}}\right\rbrack , \tag{8}\] where \( f\left( \cdot \right) \) denotes \( {L}_{2} \) normalized representations, \( {\mathrm{p}}_{{pos}\left( {\cdot , \cdot }\right) } \) represents the distribution of positive pairs, \( {x}_{i}^{ - } \) denotes negative instances,and \( \tau \) is a temperature coefficient. Current research [35,37] splits infoNCE into alignment and uniformity losses. \[{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{ infoNCE }} = {\mathcal{L}}_{\text{ alignment }} + {\mathcal{L}}_{\text{ uniformity }}\] \[= {\mathbb{E}}_{\left( {x,y}\right) \sim {\mathrm{p}}_{\text{ pos }}}\left\lbrack {-f{\left( x\right) }^{T}f\left( y\right) /\tau }\right\rbrack + {\mathbb{E}}_{\left( {x,y}\right) \sim {\mathrm{p}}_{\text{ pos }}}\log \left\lbrack {{e}^{f{\left( x\right) }^{T}f\left( y\right) /\tau } + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{e}^{f{\left( {x}_{i}^{ - }\right) }^{T}f\left( x\right) /\tau }}\right\rbrack . \tag{9}\] The alignment term aims to minimize the distance of positive pairs in the embedding space, thus enhancing the similarity between them, while the minimization of the uniformity term enhances the homogeneity of the representations. Previous work [33] treats user-item interaction pairs as positive pairs and optimizes the alignment loss to pull them closer and treats non-interacted user-item pairs as negative pairs and pushes them farther away. Work [41] has refined the theoretical connection between these two components and graph convolution. In fact, an intrinsic correlation between the BPR loss and the loss of contrast learning alignment uniformity has been developed: \[{\mathcal{L}}_{BPR} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\left( {u,i,j}\right) \in D}} - \ln \sigma \left( {{e}_{u}^{T}{e}_{i} - {e}_{u}^{T}{e}_{j}}\right) , \tag{10}\] where \( \left( {{e}_{u},{e}_{i}}\right) \) indicates that the presence of interaction is a BPR loss positive pair and no interaction between \( \left( {{e}_{u},{e}_{j}}\right) \) is a BPR loss negative pair. Thus,for sample pairs in BPR,BPR loss positive pairs are associated with contrast learning positive pairs for alignment optimization, and BPR loss negative pairs are associated with contrast learning uniformity optimization. The uniformity of the representation space greatly affects the effectiveness of the downstream task [35]. However, the BPR loss negative pair is a subtask of the uniformity optimization of the entire representation space. That is,uniformity optimization should also include \( \left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right) \) and \( \left( {{e}_{u},{e}_{{u}^{\prime }}}\right) \) . Our goal is to optimize the uniformity of the GCN block input residual representation of the target behavior in the cascaded GCN structure; specifically, we increase the distance between representations of pairs of samples by using CL to resist the influence of low-quality embeddings of upstream behaviors on the target behaviors. Therefore, assuming the optimal alignment condition while preserving the BPR loss, Equation (9) is rewritten as Equation (11).

\[{\mathcal{L}}^{\prime }{}_{\text{ infoNCE }} = - 1/\tau + {\mathbb{E}}_{\left( {x,y}\right) \sim {\mathrm{p}}_{\text{ data }}}\log \left\lbrack {{e}^{1/\tau } + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{e}^{f{\left( {x}_{i}^{ - }\right) }^{T}f\left( x\right) /\tau }}\right\rbrack , \tag{11}\] where \( {\mathrm{p}}_{\text{ data }\left( {\cdot , \cdot }\right) } \) denotes the distribution of data pairs,which also represents the output embed-dings of the GCN block on the behavior views \( {\mathcal{P}}_{K - 1} \) . The embeddings are eventually input into behavior views \( {\mathcal{P}}_{K} \) . Using CL before the target behavior residual block enhances the quality of the representation space, reflecting the emphasis placed on target behaviors in the cascading model. By eliminating random noise or dropout strategies, the primary optimization objective of CL effectively becomes uniform embedding optimization. The representation optimization objective is expressed as follows: \[{\mathcal{L}}_{EN} = {\mathbb{E}}_{\left( {e}_{i}^{K - 1},{e}_{j}^{K - 1}\right) }\log \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i,j}}{e}^{f{\left( {e}_{i}^{K - 1}\right) }^{T}f\left( {e}_{j}^{K - 1}\right) /\tau }, \tag{12}\] where \( {e}^{K - 1} \) denotes the embedding input into the positive view \( {\mathcal{P}}_{K} \) . The method demonstrates that the CL approach, derived from single-behavior multi-layer graph convolutions, yields outstanding results, even when optimizing uniformity across behaviors. ### 4.4 Model Training 4.4.1 Training Data Generation. Following the definitions of positive and negative behavior view chains we gave in Section 4.1,we construct training datasets \( \left\{ {D}_{k}^{p}\right\} \) and \( \left\{ {D}_{k}^{n}\right\} \) for positive behavior chain \( \left\{ {\mathcal{P}}_{k}\right\} \) and negative behavior view chain \( \left\{ {\mathcal{N}}_{k}\right\} \) ,respectively. For the positive behavior view chain \( \mathcal{P} \) ,we generate the training data \( {D}_{k}^{p} \) for each view \( {\mathcal{P}}_{k} \) . \[{\mathcal{D}}_{k}^{p} = \left\{ {\left( {u,i,j}\right) \mid \left( {u,i}\right) \in {\mathcal{E}}_{k},j \notin \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{K}{\mathcal{S}}_{i}\left( u\right) }\right\} , \tag{13}\] where \( {\mathcal{S}}_{i}\left( u\right) \) denotes the set of all items \( i \) that have interacted with user \( u \) in the interaction view \( {\mathcal{G}}_{i} \) . Consequently,for the positive view chain \( \left\lbrack {{\mathcal{P}}_{1},{\mathcal{P}}_{2},\ldots ,{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}\right\rbrack \) ,the corresponding generated training data chain is \( \left\lbrack {{D}_{1}^{p},{D}_{2}^{p},\ldots ,{D}_{K}^{p}}\right\rbrack \) . Similarly,for each view \( {\mathcal{P}}_{K} \) on the negative behavior view chain \( N \) , we generate the training data \( {D}_{k}^{n} \) . \[{\mathcal{D}}_{k}^{n} = \left\{ {\left( {u,i,j}\right) \mid \left( {u,i}\right) \in {\mathcal{E}}_{k},\left( {u,i}\right) \notin \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{i = k}}^{K}{\mathcal{E}}_{k},\text{ and }j \in {\mathcal{S}}_{K}\left( u\right) }\right\} , \tag{14}\] where \( {\mathcal{S}}_{K}\left( u\right) \) denotes the set of all items \( i \) that have interacted with user \( u \) in the target behavior interaction view \( {\mathcal{G}}_{K} \) . Thus,for the positive view chain \( \left\lbrack {{\mathcal{N}}_{1},{\mathcal{N}}_{2},\ldots ,{\mathcal{N}}_{K - 1}}\right\rbrack \) ,the corresponding generated training data chain is \( \left\lbrack {{D}_{1}^{n},{D}_{2}^{n},\ldots ,{D}_{K - 1}^{n}}\right\rbrack \) . 4.4.2 Prediction Filtering. The model uses the final cascaded output embeddings to obtain scores for user \( u \) and item \( i \) on interest and non-interest,respectively,via matrix multiplication: \( {R}_{p}^{ui} = {e}_{u}^{T}{e}_{i} \) and \( {R}_{n}^{ui} = {v}_{u}^{T}{v}_{i} \) . The set of all user-item pairs is represented as follows: \[\Delta = \left\{ {\left( {u,i,{R}_{p}^{ui},{R}_{n}^{ui}}\right) \mid u \in U,i \in I}\right\} . \tag{15}\]

The filtering operation is defined as Equation (16). \[\text{ Filter }\left( \Delta \right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \left\{ {\left( {u,i,{R}_{p}^{ui},{R}_{n}^{ui}}\right) \mid u \in U,i \in I}\right\} , & \text{ if }{R}_{n}^{ui} < \delta \\ \left\{ {\left( {u,i, - \infty ,{R}_{n}^{ui}}\right) \mid u \in U,i \in I}\right\} , & \text{ otherwise, } \end{array}\right. \tag{16}\] where \( \delta \) denotes the filtering threshold and \( {R}_{n}^{ui} < \delta \) signifies that the degree of user \( {u}^{\prime }s \) disinterest in item \( i \) is below the threshold. We sort the items of interest for user \( u \) based on \( {R}_{p}^{ui} \) to generate a recommendation list of length top \( - K \) for all users \( \mathcal{U} \) . This process can be expressed as follows: \[\operatorname{Result}\left( {R}_{\operatorname{top} - K}\right) = \operatorname{Rank}\left( {\operatorname{Filter}\left( \Delta \right) }\right) = \left\{ {{\left\lbrack {i}_{1},{i}_{2},\ldots ,{i}_{L}\right\rbrack }_{u} \mid {R}_{p}^{u{i}_{l}} > {R}_{p}^{u{i}_{l + 1}},u \in U}\right\} . \tag{17}\] 4.4.3 Multi-Task Training. We adopt the multi-task training framework [30], with the overall loss \( \mathcal{L} \) defined as follows: \[\mathcal{L} = {\mathcal{L}}_{CR} + \alpha \cdot {\mathcal{L}}_{EN} \tag{18}\] where \( \alpha \) denotes a hyperparameter that controls the weight of the enhancement module in the loss,and \( {\mathcal{L}}_{EN} \) denotes the representation enhancement loss,detailed in Section 4.3. \( {\mathcal{L}}_{CR} \) includes the BPR and regularization losses in both the positive and negative views. The model structure uses a multi-behavior chain with multi-level positive and negative feedback signals to learn user and item embeddings from both positive and negative interests. The positive interest embeddings are \( \left\{ {{e}_{u}^{1},{e}_{u}^{2},\ldots ,{e}_{u}^{K}}\right\} \) and \( \left\{ {{e}_{i}^{1},{e}_{i}^{2},\ldots ,{e}_{i}^{K}}\right\} \) and the negative interest embeddings are \( \left\{ {{v}_{u}^{1},{v}_{u}^{2},\ldots ,{v}_{u}^{K}}\right\} \) and \( \left\{ {{v}_{i}^{1},{v}_{i}^{2},\ldots ,{v}_{i}^{K}}\right\} \) . Consistent with CRGCN [44],we design a loss function to learn user interests for each view. The loss on the positive behavior views \( {\mathcal{P}}_{k} \) is expressed as follows: \[{\mathcal{L}}_{k}^{p} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\left( {u,i,j}\right) \in {D}_{k}^{P}}} - \ln \sigma \left( {{e}_{u}^{T}{e}_{i} - {e}_{u}^{T}{e}_{j}}\right) \tag{19}\] where \( \sigma \left( \cdot \right) \) denotes the sigmoid function and \( {\mathcal{D}}_{k}^{P} \) denotes the training dataset. Similarly,we obtain \( K \) losses \( \left\{ {{\mathcal{L}}_{1}^{p},{\mathcal{L}}_{2}^{p},\ldots ,{\mathcal{L}}_{K}^{p}}\right\} \) . Similarly,the loss on the negative behavior views \( {\mathcal{N}}_{k} \) is expressed as follows: \[{\mathcal{L}}_{k}^{n} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\left( {u,i,j}\right) \in {D}_{k}^{n}}} - \ln \sigma \left( {{v}_{u}^{T}{v}_{i} - {v}_{u}^{T}{v}_{j}}\right) \tag{20}\] Thus, the total loss on the cascading view structure is expressed as follows: \[{\mathcal{L}}_{CR} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{K}{\mathcal{L}}_{i}^{p} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{{K - 1}}{\mathcal{L}}_{i}^{n} + \beta \cdot \parallel \Theta {\parallel }_{2} \tag{21}\] where \( \parallel \Theta {\parallel }_{2} \) represents the \( {L}_{2} \) regularization term of the initial embedding,and the hyperparameter \( \beta \) controls the \( {L}_{2} \) regularization intensity. The overall loss is expressed in more detail in Equations (18)-(22): \[\mathcal{L} = \alpha \cdot {\mathcal{L}}_{EN} + {\mathcal{L}}_{CR} = \alpha \cdot {\mathbb{E}}_{\left( {e}_{i}^{K - 1},{e}_{j}^{K - 1}\right) }\log \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i,j}}{e}^{f{\left( {e}_{i}^{K - 1}\right) }^{T}f\left( {e}_{j}^{K - 1}\right) /\tau } + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{K}{\mathcal{L}}_{i}^{p} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{{K - 1}}{\mathcal{L}}_{i}^{n} + \beta \cdot \parallel \Theta {\parallel }_{2}. \tag{22}\] 4.4.4 Complexity Analysis. The trainable parameters of our proposed model are initialized with positive and negative interest embeddings for users and items, and it benefits from a simple model architecture that does not include additional trainable parameters, such as multiple feature transformation matrices, similar to MB-CGCN [4]. In addition, our model's time cost primarily comes from generating negative behavioral views, computing the adjacency matrix for each behavior, performing graph convolution,calculating the BPR loss,and optimizing the embedding loss. Let \( \left| E\right| \) be the number of edges in the user-item interaction graph, \( K \) denote the number of behavior types, \( n \) is the number of epochs, \( b \) denotes the size of each training batch, \( d \) denotes the embedding size,and \( L \) denotes the number of GCN layers.

The time complexity of generating a negative view is \( O\left( {2\left( {K - 1}\right) \left| E\right| }\right) \) . The time complexity in computing the adjacency matrix is \( O\left( {{2K}\left| E\right| + 2\left( {K - 1}\right) \left| E\right| }\right) \) . During graph convolution,the time complexity is \( O\left( {{2K}\operatorname{Ind}b{\left| E\right| }^{2} + 2\left( {K - 1}\right) \operatorname{Lnd}b{\left| E\right| }^{2}}\right) \) . The time complexity of BPR Loss is \( O({2K}\operatorname{nd}\left| E\right| + \; 2\left( {K - 1}\right) {nd}\left| E\right| \) ). The time complexity of uniformity loss for performing representation optimization is \( O\left( {{2nd}{\left| E\right| }^{2}}\right) \) . Typically,the number of behavioral species in a multi-behavioral recommendation task is usually small ( \( K = 4 \) in the Tmall dataset, \( K = 3 \) in the Beibei and Tmall-s datasets). The number of convolution layers on each behavior in our model is 1 (i.e., \( L = 1 \) ). Ignoring the difference between \( K - 1 \) and \( K \) and considering that the size of the dataset depends on \( \left| E\right| \) . Thus,the time complexity is mainly determined by the quadratic term, and the total time complexity of PPN-ARE is \( O\left( {\left( {{4Kb} + 2}\right) {nd}{\left| E\right| }^{2}}\right) \) . Notice that the time complexity of LightGCN [12] is \( O\left( {2\left| E\right| + {2Lbnd}{\left| E\right| }^{2} + {2nd}\left| E\right| }\right) \) ,where generally \( L = 3 \) ,and the time complexity of CRGCN [44] is \( O\left( {{2K}\left| E\right| + {2KLbnd}{\left| E\right| }^{2} + {2Knd}\left| E\right| }\right) \) ,suggesting that the time complexity of our model is of a similar order of magnitude to that of LightGCN and CRGCN, and thus we believe that the potential concerns about the time spend associated with the addition of learning about behavioral negative interests are within affordable limits. ## 5 Experiments In this section, we conducted extensive experiments on real-world datasets, to validate the efficacy of PNN-ARE, and address the primary research questions (RQ) outlined below: - RQ1: How does the performance of our PPN-ARE compare with the SOTA recommendation baselines? - RQ2: How does each component of our model contribute to improving recommendation performance? - RQ3: How does the design of different representation optimization layers impact the recommendation accuracy? -RQ4: How does our model respond to different contrastive learning designs? -RQ5: How would different multi-behavioral modeling orders affect learned behavioral dependencies? - RQ6: How sensitive is our model to different hyperparameters? - RQ7: How is the robustness and training efficiency of the PPN-ARE model? ### 5.1 Experimental Settings In this section, we provide a brief introduction to the experimental setup, including the datasets, comparison baselines, evaluation metrics, and details of the experimental parameters. 5.1.1 Datasets. We implement our model \( {}^{4} \) on PyTorch and conduct experiments on the following hardware platform: CPU, Intel Xeon E5-2678; GPU, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090; OS, Ubuntu 20.04.1. Training process of PPN-ARE on Beibei and Tmall datasets. ## 6 Related Work In this section, we review advances in multi-behavior recommendation and in graph convolution networks with symbolic representations. Furthermore, we provide a brief overview of recent advances in graph-contrastive learning for recommender systems.

### 6.1 Multi-Behavior Recommendation The multi-behavior recommendation has effectively mitigated data sparsity and enhanced recommendation performance,emerging as a popular research direction \( \left\lbrack {2,6,{15},{42}}\right\rbrack \) . Early research straightforwardly transplanted single-behavior models to multi-behavior data, such as applying collective matrix factorization to multiple behavior matrices through parameter sharing [31, 51] or devising novel sampling strategies to bolster training data [6, 10]. With the emergence of deep learning, GCNs have been introduced to recommendation models [4]. Such research created a unified graph, executed GCN to ascertain user-item embeddings, and subsequently aggregated these embeddings to forecast the target behavior [15, 43]. The MBGCN [15] learns behavior contributions on a unified user-item graph and models behavior semantics on an item-item collaborative interaction graph, ultimately predicting based on both. The MBGMN [43] utilizes a meta-graph neural network to model multi-behavior patterns and captures behavior heterogeneity and diversity within a unified graph. Models such as ChainRec [32] and NMTR [7] use a multi-task learning framework, treating each behavior as a prediction target and feeding the prediction from a prior behavior into the forecasting process of the next behavior. Some recent studies have sought to directly model dependencies among multiple behaviors. CRGCN [44] employs cascaded multi-task learning with residual connections to model behavioral dependencies. Furthermore, MB-CGCN [4] devises feature transformations to avoid structural issues from residual connections. PKEF [22] designed a representation projection to decouple upstream auxiliary behavioral representations to generate expert information to guide target behavior prediction. BCIPM [45] utilizes contextual information to select preferences in auxiliary behaviors for target behavior recommendations. It is noteworthy that MB-CGCN, PKEF, and BCIPM all focus on aligning or filtering preference information between behaviors. Disen-CGCN [3] also employs cascading networks for multi-behavior preference modeling, utilizing decoupling and attention mechanisms to differentially describe users' preferences across various behaviors. BPMR [17] uses a Bayesian approach for recommendation by mining behavioral patterns. POGCN [50] builds on behavioral cascade relationships and models multi-behavioral dependencies using biased order relationships to achieve better results. In general, these methods focus only on positive dependencies between behaviors and do not consider other dependencies. Therefore, we extract implicit negative feedback information to supplement and enhance inter-behavioral dependencies. ### 6.2 Graph Convolution Networks on Signed Graph Benefiting from its capability to capture high-order information, GCN [16] has emerged as a fundamental tool in recommendation systems [40]. Leveraging the message-passing mechanism of GCN, NGCF [36] yielded commendable collaborative filtering recommendation results. LightGCN [12] further simplified the model, enhancing recommendation performance. Numerous studies have adopted GCN as a cornerstone for recommendation models [4, 15, 25, 44], utilizing it to aggregate information from local neighbors. However, recent research suggests that the message-passing paradigm of GCN may not effectively handle both positive and negative feedback simultaneously [12, 21, 24], which is contrary to the real-world scenario where user feedback often exhibits multi-polar tendencies. To overcome this issue, SGCN [5] allocates balanced and imbalanced embeddings to nodes and propagates both embeddings in signed graphs based on balance theory. SiReN [28] uses both GNN and MLP to generate positive and negative embeddings for each node in the signed graph and then aggregates the two embeddings into the final representation using an attention mechanism. PANE-GNN [21] creates separate graphs for positive and negative feedback signals, utilizing GCN for information propagation in each graph. Because of its homogeneity assumption, the unified graph construction approach for multi-behavior recommendation based on GCN struggles to effectively deal with multi-level positive and negative feedback. To harness the rich feedback signals in multi-behavior interactions, our model facilitates two types of graph message propagations, segregating them based on graded positive and negative feedback.

### 6.3 Graph-Based Contrastive Learning CL is a self-supervised method based on the principle that pairs of positive samples should be more similar and pairs of negative samples should be less similar, and the representation space is optimized by comparing pairs of samples, where positive ones are represented more closely and negative ones are distanced from each other, which results in a better quality representation space. Recent work has introduced CL into recommender systems, with notable achievements in graph-based collaborative filtering research [19, 33, 39, 47, 49]. NCL [19] introduces structural and semantic neighbor information to alleviate data sparsity, whereas simGCL [47] optimizes representation quality through CL, which directly affects recommendation performance, and replaces the edge-dropout strategy with noise injection. Recent works, such as S-MBRec [8] and IICL [18], have further introduced CL into multi-behavior recommendation and yielded noticeable results. Notably, the work [37] explains the connection between graph CL and graph convolution operations, starting from CL and graph representation Learning. Recent research [35] suggests that better quality representations in graph tasks are closely related to the effectiveness of downstream tasks. Existing work on multi-behavior residual cascade recommendation \( \left\lbrack {4,{17},{44},{45},{50}}\right\rbrack \) overlooks the need to optimize representation quality in multi-behavior dependency modeling from a representation-learning perspective. PKEF [22] and Disen-CGCN [3] started to process preference representations from a representational point of view, but failed to think about it in a more detailed way from the perspective of representation learning. ## 7 Conclusion and Future Work Our work introduces an enhanced cascade GCN for multi-behavior recommendation, enriching valuable user preference information via data-layer enhancement and representation-layer optimization. First, we extract user-level cascading multi-feedback when modeling behavior dependencies to obtain richer multi-behavior preference information. Next, we design behavior view chains and simultaneously learn user multi-polar interest embeddings. Finally, we embed a representation-optimization layer within the cascade structure, optimizing end-residual inputs via CL. Our proposed model has been extensively validated through experiments on real datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness. In addition, our model outperforms SOTAs. By constructing behavior view chains, we offer an alternative approach for handling multi-behavior multi-feedback scenarios. Moreover, by comparing different representation optimization schemes, we reveal existing issues in current cascade GCNs and highlight their potential for improvement. In summary, our model not only excels in multi-behavior recommendation but also provides fresh insights into handling multi-behavior feedback information and constructing cascade GCNs. It is worth noting that certain aspects of our work require attention and future improvement. First, the representation optimization scheme can enhance inter-behavior robustness to some extent; however, research on more advanced techniques to address the low-quality embedding between behaviors and to align multi-behavior preference information remains a matter of concern. Second, our model focuses on cascading behavioral interaction models, and research on their applicability to more complex behavioral data scenarios is also necessary. In addition, not all auxiliary behaviors contribute equally to the prediction of the target behavior, information redundancy exists, and in future work, we plan to simplify the data and model. This provides a viable approach for controlling model complexity.
